steps.title: In the ground
steps.text: Vanadium is spread through certain iron ores, the titanium-bearing magnetites of China, Russia and South Africa, where it makes up less than 2% of the rock. It also occurs in oil, coal and uranium sandstone.
steps.india: 64,594 t of vanadium pentoxide in iron-ore resources, and 81,300 t of vanadium oxide found with rare earths in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

steps.title: Mine with iron
steps.text: Most vanadium is a co-product of steel. The magnetite is mined as iron ore and smelted in a blast furnace; vanadium dissolves in the molten iron. Blowing oxygen through the iron then moves it into a slag, which is skimmed off.

steps.title: Roast and leach
steps.text: The slag is roasted with soda or salt at about 1,000°C, which turns vanadium into a form that dissolves in water. It is leached out, precipitated with ammonium salts and heated to give vanadium pentoxide flake.
steps.alt: A second supply comes from waste: oil-refinery residues, spent catalysts and power-station ash are leached the same way.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: Most pentoxide is reduced with aluminium, in a reaction that supplies its own heat, to make ferrovanadium for steelmakers. Purer oxide is dissolved in sulphuric acid as battery electrolyte, or alloyed with aluminium for titanium alloys.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: More than 90% goes into steel. A fraction of a per cent makes reinforcing bar and structural steel much stronger. Vanadium catalysts make sulphuric acid, and vanadium flow batteries store grid power for hours.
steps.india: By-products from steel slag and petroleum ash meet 20 to 30% of consumption; the rest is imported.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Vanadium returns in alloy-steel scrap. Spent refinery catalysts are processed for vanadium, molybdenum and nickel. Flow-battery electrolyte does not wear out and can be reused.

sources.title: Takshashila, India Critical Minerals: scores, project records and capability notes (2026)
